# blitz-format

@difference Extension: `blitz-format` formats `.bb` source code (indentation, keyword case, spacing, blank lines, line endings) from a `.blitz-format` file; the original has no formatter.

`blitz-format` applies one style to BlitzBasic, Blitz3D and BlitzPlus source code, so that a project reads the same everywhere. It changes white space, blank lines, line endings and the case of keywords, and nothing else: Names, numbers, strings and comments keep their text, and the formatted program is the same program. Every result is compared with its input token by token before it is written, and a result that differs is refused with an error, so a mistake of the formatter can not change a program.

```text
blitz-format [options] [file...]
```

Files are rewritten in place, and the only output is the name of each file, one per line (files that were already formatted are not touched, but are named too). Without files (or with `-`) the standard input is formatted and the result is written to the standard output. These options change that:

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-r`, `--recursive` | A directory on the command line means every `.bb` file beneath it (not case sensitive, sorted by path). Other files are ignored, as `.b3d` is a 3D model format as well. Without `-r` a directory is an error. Files given by name are always used, whatever their extension. |
| `--check` | Write the names of the files that would change, and exit with 1 if there are any. Nothing is written to the files, and no other name is written. |
| `--diff` | Write a unified diff of the changes, and exit with 1 if there are any. Nothing is written to the files. |
| `-q`, `--quiet` | Don't write the names of the files. Errors are still written. |
| `-i`, `--in-place` | Does nothing, as files are always rewritten in place. It is accepted so that older command lines keep working. |
| `--config=FILE` | Read the settings from this file instead of looking for one. |
| `--no-config` | Don't read a configuration file. |
| `--stdin-filepath=PATH` | The name of the standard input, shown in `--check` and `--diff` and used to find the configuration file. |
| `--print-config` | Write the settings that would be used, in the format of `.blitz-format`. |
| `--KEY=VALUE` | Set one of the settings below. `--KEY` alone sets a yes/no setting to `true`, and `--no-KEY` to `false`. `-` and `_` are the same in `KEY`. |
| `-h`, `--help`, `-v`, `--version` | Help and version. |

The exit code is 0 when everything went well, 1 when `--check` or `--diff` found a file that would change, and 2 when a file or a setting was refused. A file that can't be formatted doesn't stop the others.

```text
blitz-format -r src               # format every source file of a project
blitz-format src/*.bb             # format some files
blitz-format < main.bb            # standard input to standard output
blitz-format -r --check src       # in a CI job: fails when a file is not formatted
blitz-format --diff main.bb       # look at what would change
blitz-format --indent-style=space --indent-width=2 main.bb
```

## Settings

The settings come from a file next to the source code, and the command line overrides the file. For each file the directory of the file is searched for `.blitz-format` and then `blitz-format.json`, then its parent directory, and so on up to the root of the drive. The first file found is used, and the other files are not read, so a project keeps one file in its top directory and a subfolder can have its own.

`.blitz-format` is a list of `key = value` lines, and lines that start with `#` or `;` are comments:

```text
# Spaces, like the rest of the project
indent_style = space
indent_width = 2
keyword_case = capitalized
operator_spacing = spaced
```

`blitz-format.json` is a JSON object with the same keys, where yes/no settings can be `true` and `false` and numbers can be numbers. (The two kinds of file are told apart by their first character, so either name can hold either.)

```json
{
  "indent_style": "space",
  "indent_width": 2,
  "max_blank_lines": 2
}
```

Names are not case sensitive. Every setting has a default, which is used when nothing sets it:

| Setting | Values | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `indent_style` | tab \| space | `tab` | Indent with one tab per level, or with indent_width spaces. |
| `indent_width` | 1 - 16 | `4` | Spaces per level when indent_style is space. |
| `indent_case` | true \| false | `true` | Put Case and Default one level in from Select, so that the code under them is two levels in. |
| `indent_labels` | true \| false | `false` | Put .label lines at the indent of the code around them. Otherwise they start in the first column. |
| `keyword_case` | preserve \| lower \| upper \| capitalized | `capitalized` | How keywords are written: if, IF, If. Capitalized is the spelling of the manuals (If, EndIf, Wend). Names and commands are never changed. |
| `operator_spacing` | preserve \| spaced \| compact | `spaced` | Spaces around + - * / ^ = < > <= >= <>. Compact removes them. Mod, And, Or, Xor, Shl, Shr and Sar always have spaces. A sign (-1) never has a space behind it. |
| `separator_spacing` | preserve \| spaced \| compact | `spaced` | Spaces around the : between statements. |
| `comma_space` | true \| false | `true` | A space behind each comma, and none in front of it. |
| `paren_inner_space` | true \| false | `false` | A space behind ( and in front of ). |
| `paren_space` | preserve \| never | `preserve` | Never removes the space in Name (x) so that it reads Name(x). Keywords (If (x)) keep their space either way. |
| `comment_gap` | 0 - 16 | `1` | Spaces between code and a comment behind it. 0 keeps the space that is there, which keeps comments that are lined up in a column. |
| `comment_space` | true \| false | `false` | Add a space after the ; when the comment starts with a letter or a digit. ;;; and ;---- are left alone. |
| `max_empty_lines` | -1 - 100 | `1` | The most empty lines in a row, also between statements. More are removed. -1 allows any number. This was called `max_blank_lines`, which still works. |
| `blank_lines_around_declarations` | 0 - 10 | `1` | Blank lines to have before a Function or Type (above the comments that belong to it) and after its End. 0 leaves them alone. |
| `align_assignments` | true \| false | `false` | Line up the `=` of assignments on consecutive lines. See [Alignment](#alignment). |
| `align_declares` | true \| false | `false` | Line up the names and the `=` of `Const`, `Dim`, `Local` and `Global` on consecutive lines. See [Alignment](#alignment). |
| `trim_trailing_space` | true \| false | `true` | Remove spaces and tabs at the end of lines (also in comments). |
| `final_newline` | true \| false | `true` | End the file with a line break, and remove blank lines at the end. |
| `line_ending` | auto \| lf \| crlf \| cr | `auto` | Auto uses what the first line break of the file is, or lf if there is none. |

## What the style does

Blocks are indented by one level: The body of a `Function`, `Type`, `If` (block form), `ElseIf`/`Else`, `For`, `While`, `Repeat` and `Select`. `Case` and `Default` are one level in from `Select` unless `indent_case` is off. An `If` with its statement on the same line (`If a Then b Else c`) has no block. The statements on a line that are separated by `:` count one after the other, so `For i = 1 To 3 : Print i : Next` stays on one line and doesn't change the indentation after it. Code that doesn't match up (a `Next` without a `For`) never indents below the first column.

Before:

```blitzbasic
Type  Point
Field x#,y#
 End Type
function Sign%( n% )
  if n<0 then return -1
  IF n>0 Then Return  1
  Return 0
end function
Select total
Case -1,-2
Print "negative"
  Default
   Print "other"
End Select
For i=1 To 3:total=total+Sign(i)*2:Next
```

After:

```blitzbasic
Type Point
	Field x#, y#
End Type

Function Sign%(n%)
	If n < 0 Then Return -1
	If n > 0 Then Return 1
	Return 0
End Function

Select total
	Case -1, -2
		Print "negative"
	Default
		Print "other"
End Select
For i = 1 To 3 : total = total + Sign(i) * 2 : Next
```

Keywords are the words of the language (`If`, `EndIf`, `Wend`, `Mod`, `And`, `Int`...). Names of variables, functions and commands are never changed, and neither is a field that has the name of a keyword (`p\Last`). `capitalized` writes the spelling of the manuals (`If`, `ElseIf`, `EndIf`, `Wend`). Whether `EndIf` is one word or two (`End If`) stays as it was written.

A `-` or `+` in front of a value (`x = -1`, `Case -1`, `Step -1`) is a sign and stays close to its number. After a name that is not a keyword with a space in front and none behind (`Print -1`, `a -1`) it could be a sign or a subtraction, so the spacing around it stays as it was written.

Comments, strings and numbers keep their text. The only thing that changes in a comment is the white space at the end (with `trim_trailing_space`), and a missing space after the `;` if `comment_space` is on.

## Alignment

`align_assignments` and `align_declares` line up lines that follow each other, with the same indent. A blank line, a comment line, a line of another kind or a line that is indented differently ends the group. They are off by default.

```blitzbasic
a=1
longer=2
p\x=3
Const A=1
Local Longer:Int32=2
Global b=3
Dim arr(5)
```

becomes, with `align_assignments = true` and `align_declares = true`,

```blitzbasic
a      = 1
longer = 2
p\x    = 3
Const  A            = 1
Local  Longer:Int32 = 2
Global b            = 3
Dim    arr(5)
```

* Lines with more than one statement (`a = 1 : b = 2`) are left alone, and so is an `If` with its statement on the same line: there is no telling which `=` to line up. They end the group.
* A declaration of several variables (`Local a, b = 1`) has its name lined up with the others, but its `=` stays where it is.
* A comment behind the code stays behind the code.

## Notes

* A `Function` or `Type` that is not inside another block counts as a declaration. `blank_lines_around_declarations` puts blank lines above it (above the comment lines directly over it, which belong to it) and below its `End`.
* The result is stable: Formatting the formatted text doesn't change it.
* The compiler is the judge of what a program means. `blitz-format` doesn't compile anything, so it formats code that has errors, too.
